head: Named after the Caledonian Asylum, a home for Scottish children.
text: The asylum was set up for children of Scottish soldiers and sailors killed or wounded in the Napoleonic Wars, and moved to this road in 1828. 'Caledonia' is the old Latin name for Scotland.

head: Named after the Caledonian Asylum, and Barnsbury, the manor of the Berners family.
text: The asylum was a home for Scottish children ('Caledonia' is Latin for Scotland). Barnsbury recalls the de Berners family, who held the manor in the Middle Ages.

head: Despite the name, Cambridge Heath has nothing to do with Cambridge.
text: It was recorded in 1275 as Camprichesheth; the first part is probably an old personal name. Over time it was changed to look like the familiar 'Cambridge'.

head: Named after Camden Road, which honours Charles Pratt, 1st Earl Camden.
text: He owned the land of Camden Town. His title came from Camden Place, his house in Kent, named after the historian William Camden.

head: Named after Charles Pratt, 1st Earl Camden, who owned the land.
text: In 1791 he began to let it for building houses. His title came from Camden Place, his house in Kent, which had been named after the historian William Camden.

head: Named after a lake that was once part of Canada Dock.
text: The dock in the Surrey Docks was named after the country, because most of its ships came from Canada, carrying timber. When the docks closed, it was mostly filled in, and the station opened in 1999.

head: Named after a warehouse for fruit from the Canary Islands.
text: Fruit ships from the islands unloaded here from the 1930s. The islands themselves are said to be named after dogs (Latin canis), which fits nicely: Canary Wharf is on the Isle of Dogs.

head: Probably named after a Canning, but nobody is sure which one.
text: One theory points to Charles Canning, Viceroy of India, but the name was in use before he became famous. Others suggest his father, Prime Minister George Canning, or a local firm called Canning.

head: 'Cannon' has nothing to do with guns: it comes from candle-makers.
text: In the Middle Ages this was Candelwrichtestrete, the street of the candle-wrights. Over time the name was shortened to Cannon Street.

head: 'Canonbury' means the manor of the canons.
text: The canons of St Bartholomew's Priory held the land in the Middle Ages. Canonbury Tower, built in the 16th century, still stands.

head: Named after the canons of St Bartholomew's Priory, who owned land here.
text: After Henry VIII closed the priory, the estate passed to private owners. In the early 18th century the Duke of Chandos built a grand house here called Cannons, which was pulled down in 1747. Its grounds became Canons Park.

head: Probably named after a family called Carpender, who held land here.
text: The area stayed rural until a large housing estate was built in the 1950s.

head: 'Chadwell' means the cold spring.
text: It was recorded in 1254 as Chaudewell, from Old English ceald, cold, and wella, spring. The heath beside it was open common land.

head: Named after the villages of Chalfont and Latimer.
text: 'Chalfont' probably means the chalk stream, from Old English cealc funta. Latimer is named after the Latimer family, who held the land from the early 14th century. The station was called Chalfont Road until 1915.

head: 'Chalk' has nothing to do with chalk: the name comes from Chalcot Farm.
text: Chalcot may come from Old English words for 'cold cottages'. The farm was a local landmark about 200 years ago.

head: Named after the Chancery, a royal office and court of medieval England.
text: The Chancery kept the king's records and dealt with matters of fairness in law. The lane is still at the heart of legal London, near the Inns of Court.

head: 'Charing' probably means a bend, and the Cross is a memorial to a queen.
text: The name may come from Old English cierring, a turning, perhaps the bend in the Thames. Edward I put up a cross here for his wife Eleanor, who died in 1290. A Victorian copy stands in front of the main line station.

head: 'Chesham' means the river meadow by a heap of stones.
text: It was recorded about a century before the Norman Conquest as Cæstæleshamm. Chesham is the end of a single-track branch of the Metropolitan line.

head: 'Cheshunt' probably means the spring by the old Roman fort.
text: It comes from Old English ceaster, a Roman fort or town, and funta, a spring. The Domesday Book of 1086 records it as Cestrehunt.

head: Nobody is quite sure what 'Chigwell' means.
text: It may be the well or spring of a man called Cicca, or it may come from a different word altogether. The village sits on the edge of Epping Forest.

head: 'Chingford' probably means the shingle ford.
text: The ford crossed the River Lea over a stony bed. On the edge of Epping Forest stands Queen Elizabeth's Hunting Lodge, built for Henry VIII in 1543.

head: 'Chiswick' means the cheese farm.
text: The Old English name points to a farm making cheese near the Thames. The station opened in 1879 as Acton Green and became Chiswick Park in 1910.

head: 'Chorley' probably means a clearing of the ceorls, free peasants.
text: Ceorl is the Old English word that gave us 'churl'. The 'wood' part needs no explanation. The station was called Chorley Wood, in two words, until 1964.

head: Named after Clapham's common, a large open space.
text: 'Clapham' probably means the homestead near a hill or hillock, from Old English clopp; another idea is a man called Cloppa. The common was once rough grazing land and is now a public park.

head: Named after Clapham's high street; 'Clapham' probably means the homestead near a hill.
text: The Old English name may come from clopp, a lump or hillock. The station was called Clapham until 1989.

head: Named after Clapham, though the station is actually in Battersea.
text: When it opened in 1863, Clapham was the smarter-sounding name. It is one of the busiest railway stations in Europe by number of trains.

head: Named after Clapham, probably the homestead near a hill.
text: The Old English name may come from clopp, a lump or hillock, or from a man called Cloppa. This station opened in 1900 as Clapham Road and was renamed Clapham North in 1926.

head: Named after Clapham, probably the homestead near a hill.
text: It opened in 1926; 'Nightingale Lane' had been considered as its name. Under the station is one of eight deep-level shelters built during the Second World War.

head: 'Clapton' means the farm on a hill.
text: It comes from Old English clopp, a lump or hill, and tūn, farm. The area runs down to the River Lea and the Hackney Marshes.

head: Nobody knows for sure where 'Cockfosters' comes from.
text: It is first recorded in the 16th century. A popular idea is that it was the home of the 'cock forester', the chief forester of the royal hunting ground of Enfield Chase.

head: The name is thought to recall the Collin family, landowners in the 16th century.
text: Colindale was farmland until the 20th century; it is now home to the RAF Museum on the site of Hendon aerodrome.

head: Named after a wood used by colliers, or charcoal burners.
text: In the past a collier was someone who made charcoal, not a coal miner. The wood survived into the late 19th century.

head: 'Covent' is an old form of 'convent'.
text: In the Middle Ages this was the garden of Westminster Abbey. The famous fruit and vegetable market began here in the 17th century and moved to Nine Elms in 1974.

head: The name refers to a crossing of Millwall Dock nearby.
text: For some years the station was called Crossharbour and London Arena, after a sports and concert hall that has since been demolished.

head: 'Crouch' is an old word for a cross: the hill with a cross.
text: Middle English crouche meant cross, probably a wayside cross. The same word is in nearby Crouch End.

head: 'Croxley' probably means the clearing of a man called Crocc.
text: Leah, a clearing in a wood, is one of the most common endings in English place names. The station opened in 1925 as Croxley Green and was renamed Croxley in 1949.

head: Named after the Crystal Palace, the huge glass building of the Great Exhibition of 1851.
text: It was moved here from Hyde Park and reopened in 1854. It burnt down in 1936, but the Victorian dinosaur sculptures in the park survive.

head: Named after a custom house at the Royal Victoria Dock, where duty was paid on goods.
text: Ships unloading in the Royal Docks had their cargoes checked and taxed here. Today the station serves the ExCeL exhibition centre.

head: Named after the Cutty Sark, a tea clipper of 1869, now a museum ship nearby.
text: 'Cutty sark' is Scots for a short nightdress: the ship was named after the witch Nannie in Robert Burns's poem Tam o' Shanter, who wears one. Her figure is on the ship's bow.

head: Named after the island of Cyprus, which came under British control in 1878.
text: Houses for workers at the Royal Docks and the Beckton gasworks were built here at the time, and the patriotic name stuck. Little remains of the old estate.

head: 'Dagenham' means the homestead of a Saxon called Dæcca.
text: It was first written down in 666 as Dæccanhaam, in a charter of Barking Abbey. The station opened in 1902 as Dagenham and became Dagenham East in 1949.

head: Named after Dagenham and the Heathway, the road to Becontree Heath.
text: Dagenham means the homestead of a Saxon called Dæcca. The station opened in 1932 as plain Heathway, to serve the new Becontree estate, and added 'Dagenham' in 1949.

head: 'Dalston' means the farm of a man called Deorlaf.
text: It was recorded in 1294 as Derleston. The station closed in 1986 and reopened in 2010 for the new East London line.

head: 'Kingsland' means the king's land.
text: It was recorded in 1395 as Kyngeslond, probably royal land used for hunting. Dalston means the farm of a man called Deorlaf.

head: 'Debden' means the deep valley.
text: The valley is that of the River Roding. The station first opened in 1865 on a railway line and was called Chigwell Lane until 1949, when the Central line took it over.

head: Said to be named after Prince George of Denmark, husband of Queen Anne.
text: He is supposed to have had a house or hunted here around 1700. King's College Hospital is next to the station.

head: 'Deptford' means the deep ford.
text: The ford crossed the River Ravensbourne, later replaced by a bridge. Deptford was home to a royal dockyard founded by Henry VIII.

head: Named after Devons Road, the street beside the station.
text: Where the street's own name comes from is not recorded. The station opened with the first DLR line in 1987.

head: Nobody is quite sure where 'Dollis Hill' comes from.
text: One idea is a local family called Dalley. In the Second World War the Post Office Research Station here built Colossus, one of the first electronic computers, for the codebreakers at Bletchley Park. Churchill's emergency bunker, 'Paddock', is also nearby.

head: 'Ealing' means the people of a Saxon called Gilla.
text: The name, first recorded around 700 as Gillingas, slowly turned into Ylling and then Ealing. A 'broadway' is a wide main street, here the town's shopping street.

head: Named after the common, a stretch of open grassland in Ealing.
text: 'Ealing' means the people of a Saxon called Gilla. The station was called Ealing Common and West Acton for a time, from 1886 to 1910.

head: Named after the court of the Earls of Oxford, lords of the manor.
text: The de Vere family, Earls of Oxford, held the land from soon after the Norman Conquest for about 500 years. Their manor court, where local disputes were settled, stood near the station.

head: 'Acton' means the farm by the oak trees.
text: It comes from Old English āc, oak, and tūn, farm. East Acton was a separate hamlet east of the town, and its station opened in 1920.
